title: The Question Behind the Question. Learning to Hear What Is Actually Being Asked
body: A colleague asked me last month whether our backup runs at night. I said yes, at two. He nodded and left, and I felt the small satisfaction of a question answered. Two weeks later we lost a day of work to a sync failure, and I finally understood that his question had never been about two in the morning. The question behind the question is a skill I learned late and expensively, and it is not the mystical thing communication workshops make it. It is arithmetic. A person asks the question they think you can answer. The need underneath is often bigger, and the gap between the asked question and the actual need is where all the trouble lives. The backup question decoded. What he needed was whether his work could survive a machine death before a deadline. The two in the morning answer was true and useless. The useful answer was, your folder syncs hourly and I will show you how to check it yourself right now. I gave the first answer. The gap cost a day. Case two, from my partner, perfectly innocent. Asking what time I would be home. For years I answered with times. Seven, probably, eight at the latest. The question was never a schedule inquiry. It was a coordination request wearing a time costume. What she was actually asking was, do I plan dinner around you or without you, and can I tell the children a promise that will hold. The times I gave were forecasts. The answer needed was a commitment, and the difference between a forecast and a commitment is the difference between weather and a roof. Case three, the most instructive, from a job interview, where I was the one asking. I asked a candidate a technical question and he answered a different one, fluently, and my first instinct was that he had dodged. On a second look he had answered the question behind my question. I had asked how he would optimize a slow query. What I was really asking was, when something breaks, what do you do first. He answered that. He said he would check whether it was slow recently or slow forever, because the answers have different owners. I hired him, and for two years he has been the person on the team who answers what people need, which made meetings shorter. The mechanics, for anyone wanting the practice. When a question lands, ask yourself one silent thing. What would this person do with a perfect answer. If you cannot picture them doing anything with it, you have the wrong question. The backup colleague would sleep better with a self-serve check. The partner would act differently on a commitment than on a forecast. If you can picture the action, answer toward the action, and add the literal answer as a footnote. The failure mode is real and worth naming. Answering the question behind the question can become condescension, where you decide you know better than the words. The guardrail is to answer both, briefly, and then check. Here is the time, and here is my commitment, and tell me if you wanted one or the other. The check converts mind reading into service. I still get it wrong about once a week, and the failures now have a flavor I recognize quickly. The answer was true and the room did not move. True but unmoving. That is the signature. The question behind the question is the one that moves the room, and the room is always telling you, if you watch, which question that was.
